title: ITIL (Version 5) Foundation
subtitle: Digital product and service management
source: Structured on the official ITIL Foundation (Version 5) syllabus, PeopleCert, February 2026. Definitions paraphrased.
description: Every syllabus category for the ITIL Foundation (Version 5) exam: terms, relationships, four dimensions, lifecycle, Value System, 34 practices, continual improvement, value streams, AI, DevOps and PRINCE2.

chapters.title: About ITIL (Version 5) and the exam
chapters.summary: What ITIL is, what changed from ITIL 4, and how the Foundation exam works.

blocks.text: ITIL is the most widely used body of guidance for managing IT-enabled products and services. It started in the UK government in the late 1980s, moved to AXELOS in 2013 and is owned by **PeopleCert** since 2021. **ITIL (Version 5)** was launched in early 2026; the Foundation exam went live on **12 February 2026**.

Version 5 reframes ITIL from IT service management to **digital product and service management (DPSM)**: managing products and services together, across their whole lifecycle, with value co-created with consumers.

blocks.title: About this book
blocks.text: This book follows the official ITIL Foundation (Version 5) syllabus (February 2026). Definitions are paraphrased, not quoted from the copyrighted official book. The exam uses the book's exact wording, so check key definitions against the official ITIL Foundation (Version 5) publication before your exam.

rows: Service Value System with 6 value-chain activities (plan, improve, engage, design and transition, obtain/build, deliver and support)

Of product and service management; AI included in the dimensions

Experience, UX, CX, experience level agreements, human-centred design

chapters.title: Key terms: products, services and value
chapters.summary: The vocabulary behind 30% of the exam: products, services, goods, value, outcomes, costs, risks, utility, warranty.

blocks.text: The management of products and services that are created, delivered or enabled by digital technology, across their lifecycle, so that value is co-created with consumers.
A configuration of an organisation's resources designed to offer value to a consumer. A product is what the provider has; services are how consumers get value from it.
A means of enabling value co-creation by facilitating outcomes that customers want to achieve, without the customer having to manage specific costs and risks.
A product whose value is created or delivered mainly through digital technology (software, data, platforms).
A service delivered and consumed through digital channels and technology.
A tangible or intangible resource whose ownership is transferred to the consumer, who then takes responsibility for its use (e.g. a laptop, a licence).
A recurring organisational activity at all levels to ensure performance continually meets stakeholders' expectations.
The model of eight activities (discover, design, acquire, build, transition, operate, deliver, support) that organisations combine to manage products and services from idea to retirement.

blocks.title: Product vs service
blocks.text: A bank's mobile app platform is a **product** (a configuration of software, infrastructure, people and data). "Pay a merchant by QR code" is a **service** enabled by it: the customer gets the outcome without managing the costs and risks of running payment infrastructure.

sections.title: Value, outcomes, outputs, costs and risks

blocks.text: The perceived benefits, usefulness and importance of something. Value is subjective and depends on the stakeholder.
Value is created jointly by the provider and consumer through their interactions, not delivered one-way.
A tangible or intangible deliverable of an activity.
A result for a stakeholder enabled by one or more outputs.
The amount of money spent on a specific activity or resource. Services can remove costs from the consumer (e.g. no servers to buy) or impose them (e.g. licence fees, training).

A possible event that could cause harm or loss, or make it more difficult to achieve objectives; also defined as uncertainty of outcome. Services remove some risks from consumers and may introduce others.

blocks.title: Output vs outcome
blocks.text: Output = what is produced (a report, a configured laptop). Outcome = the result the stakeholder cares about (a better decision, an employee productive on day one). Exam questions test this distinction often.

rows: The functionality offered by a product or service to meet a particular need
What does it do? (fit for purpose)
Assurance that a product or service will meet agreed requirements, such as availability, capacity, security, continuity
How well does it do it? (fit for use)
How the user perceives and responds to using the product or service
How does it feel to use?
Meeting present needs without compromising the future: environmental, social and economic
Can it be provided responsibly over time?

blocks.text: All four contribute to value co-creation: a service with great utility but poor warranty (often down) or poor experience will not be perceived as valuable.
A formal description of one or more services designed to address the needs of a target consumer group. It may include goods, access to resources and service actions.

rows: Ownership is transferred to the consumer
A hardware security key shipped to each user
Ownership is not transferred; access is granted under agreed terms
Actions performed by the provider to address a consumer need

blocks.text: Any interaction between provider and consumer during which value is co-created, such as onboarding, requesting, using, getting support or giving feedback.

rows: A person's perception of and response to their interactions with an organisation, product or service
Experience formed through digital channels and technology
Confidence that a party will act as expected; built over repeated interactions
Experience of the person using the product or service
Experience of the customer across all interactions with the provider, including buying and billing
An agreement defining targets based on experience (e.g. user satisfaction, productivity), complementing SLAs based on technical metrics
Designing products and services around the needs, abilities and behaviour of the people who use them
A plan of how to achieve long-term goals
How the organisation competes and creates value / how it uses digital technology to do so
What we do now / where we want to be / why we exist
Volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity: the conditions organisations operate in
Guiding people towards goals and shaping culture
Addition, modification or removal of anything that could affect products or services
A significant, organisation-wide change to how value is created
Normal day-to-day operations, as opposed to change or transformation work

chapters.title: Service relationships
chapters.summary: Providers, consumers, vendors, roles, relationship types, journeys, quality and SLAs.

blocks.text: A person or group of people that has its own functions with responsibilities, authorities and relationships to achieve its objectives.
The role an organisation plays when it provides services to consumers.
The role an organisation plays when it consumes services.
An organisation that creates and sells digital products (e.g. software, platforms) that others use to provide or consume services, without necessarily providing the service itself.

rows: Roles, not organisation types. The same organisation is a provider to its customers and a consumer of its suppliers.
A provider operates services for consumers; a vendor supplies products that someone else may operate.
A consumer uses services to achieve outcomes; a vendor sells products and may never see how they are used.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: A telecom operator buys a billing platform from a software vendor (digital product vendor), runs it in its own data centre, and provides mobile services to customers (service provider). It is also a service consumer of its cloud and energy suppliers.

headers: Example in a hospital buying a scheduling service
rows: Defines requirements for the service and takes responsibility for outcomes of service consumption

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: One person can hold all three roles (e.g. an individual buying a streaming service). Questions often describe a person and ask which role they play.

rows: Standard products and services; provider defines them; limited interaction and customisation
A public cloud storage subscription bought online
Services tailored to some degree; more interaction, agreed service levels, shared targets
A managed desktop service for a mid-size company with agreed SLAs
Strategic partnership; shared goals and risks; joint design and improvement
A bank and a technology partner co-designing a digital banking platform

blocks.text: The end-to-end sequence of interactions a consumer has with a provider and its products and services, from first contact through use to the end of the relationship.
The totality of a service's characteristics relevant to its ability to satisfy stated and implied needs.
One or more metrics that define expected or achieved service quality.
A documented agreement between a service provider and a customer that identifies both the services required and the expected level of service.
Feedback and value co-creation

Feedback from consumers at every interaction tells the provider whether value is being realised. It is the bridge between service interactions and improvement: without it, providers optimise what they measure, not what consumers value.

blocks.title: The watermelon effect
blocks.text: SLAs can be green while users are unhappy (green outside, red inside). This is why ITIL (Version 5) pairs SLAs with experience measures such as XLAs and feedback.

chapters.title: The Four Dimensions
chapters.summary: Organisations and people, information and technology, partners and suppliers, value streams and processes, plus PESTLE.

blocks.text: To manage products and services holistically, ITIL requires every product, service, practice and value stream to be considered from four dimensions. Neglect one and the others fail.

rows: Structures, roles, culture, competencies, leadership, and how people work with AI
Who is accountable? Do people have the skills? Does the culture support collaboration?
Information, knowledge, data, and the technologies (including AI) used to create and manage products and services
What data is needed? Which platforms and tools? How is AI used and governed?
Relationships with other organisations involved in design, delivery and support
What do we source? What are the contracts, dependencies and risks?
How parts of the organisation work together to create value; workflows and activities
What steps turn demand into value? Where are the delays?

blocks.title: AI in the dimensions
blocks.text: In Version 5, AI appears in the dimensions: organisations and people covers how people and AI work together; information and technology introduces the ITIL AI Capability Model.

The dimensions are interdependent. Buying a new ITSM tool (information and technology) fails if roles aren't clear (organisations and people), the vendor contract lacks support terms (partners and suppliers), or the incident workflow isn't redesigned (value streams and processes).

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: A company rolls out an AI service-desk assistant. Technology works, but agents don't trust it and bypass it (people), the vendor changes the model without notice (suppliers), and the escalation path to humans is unclear (processes). Value isn't realised until all four are addressed.
External factors constrain and influence all four dimensions:

rows: Government digital policies, data localisation priorities
Budgets, currency fluctuations, cost of cloud
User expectations for mobile-first, 24/7 service; workforce demographics
AI, cloud, automation, new security threats
Data protection law, AI regulation, sector rules
Energy use of data centres, sustainability reporting

chapters.title: The Product and Service Lifecycle
chapters.summary: The eight activities, their purposes, and the key terms defined within them.

blocks.text: The ITIL Product and Service Lifecycle has eight activities: **discover, design, acquire, build, transition, operate, deliver, support**. They are **not sequential or linear**. Organisations combine them iteratively into value streams; a small change may touch only transition and operate, while a new product may cycle through all eight many times.

blocks.title: Memory aid
blocks.text: **D**iscover, **D**esign, **A**cquire, **B**uild, **T**ransition, **O**perate, **D**eliver, **S**upport: "Don't Delay A Better Transition; Operate, Deliver, Support."

rows: Understand stakeholder needs, opportunities, demand and context; generate and evaluate ideas for new or changed products and services
Turn needs into product and service designs, including specifications, prototypes and experience design
Obtain the components, resources, products and services needed, from internal teams or partners and suppliers
Create, configure, integrate and test the components of products and services
Move new or changed products and services into live use safely: release, deploy and manage change
Keep technology and components running reliably and efficiently; monitor and manage events and incidents
Provide services to users day to day, fulfil service requests, and enable value realisation
Help users and restore normal service; manage problems, errors and disasters

blocks.title: What to know
blocks.text: The exam asks you to recognise each activity's purpose (Bloom's level 1) and to understand that activities are iterative. Key success metrics for each activity are also in scope; think of them as "is this activity creating value?", e.g. time to discover validated ideas, build quality, change success rate, availability, request fulfilment time, time to restore.
A description of what a product must do and how it must perform, used to guide its build.
An early, simplified version of a product used to test ideas and gather feedback before full build.
An activity that checks whether a product or service meets requirements and expectations.
A version of a product, service or component, or a collection of them, made available for use.
Frequently merging code changes into a shared repository, with automated build and test on each change.
Keeping software always in a releasable state so it can be deployed to production at any time, with deployment usually triggered by a decision.
Automatically deploying every change that passes the pipeline to production, without manual approval.

blocks.title: Delivery vs deployment
blocks.text: Continuous delivery = ready to deploy at any time (human decides). Continuous deployment = deployed automatically.
Any change of state that has significance for the management of a product, service or component.
An unplanned interruption to a service or a reduction in its quality.
The ability of a product, service or component to perform its intended function for a specified time or number of cycles.
An approach that applies software engineering to operations, using service level objectives and error budgets to balance reliability and change.
The ability to understand the internal state of a system from its external outputs, such as logs, metrics and traces.
A request from a user or an authorised representative that initiates a service action agreed as a normal part of service delivery (e.g. password reset, access request).
A cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents.
A flaw or vulnerability that may cause incidents.
A problem that has been analysed but has not been resolved.
A sudden, unplanned event that causes great damage or serious loss, typically triggering continuity plans.

blocks.title: Problem, error, known error
blocks.text: Users report slow payments (incidents). The team opens a problem. Analysis finds a memory leak in a service (the error). They document it with a workaround, restart nightly, making it a known error until a fix is released.

quiz.explain: Continuous deployment has no manual approval step.

chapters.title: The ITIL Value System
chapters.summary: Components, the seven guiding principles, governance, value chain and operating model.

sections.title: Components of the ITIL Value System

blocks.text: The **ITIL Value System** describes how all the components and activities of an organisation work together to enable value creation through products and services. Its components:

rows: Recommendations that guide decisions in all circumstances
The means by which the organisation is directed and controlled
The activities (expressed through the Product and Service Lifecycle) that respond to demand and create value
Sets of organisational resources for performing work or accomplishing objectives
A recurring activity at all levels ensuring performance keeps meeting expectations

blocks.text: Purpose: remove silos, give a flexible, integrated model where opportunity and demand are turned into value.

rows: Everything should link, directly or indirectly, to value for stakeholders
Know who the consumer is and what they value; consider experience
Don't start from scratch; assess what exists and reuse it
Observe directly; use measurement carefully; avoid assumptions
Work in small, manageable steps with feedback loops
Timebox, gather feedback at each iteration, adjust
Work across boundaries; make work and results visible
Involve the right stakeholders; share information transparently
No component works in isolation; consider the whole system
Use the four dimensions; consider end-to-end value streams
Use the minimum number of steps; remove what doesn't add value
Question each step and control; outcome-based thinking
Maximise the value of work; then automate where it helps
Optimise before automating; don't automate a bad process

blocks.title: How they interact
blocks.text: Principles are applied together, not in isolation. Example: focus on value + keep it simple decides what to remove; start where you are + progress iteratively shapes the roadmap; optimise and automate should follow simplification. Not all principles are relevant to every decision.
The means by which an organisation is directed and controlled.
Governance is **enabling**, not only restrictive: it sets direction and constraints so that teams can act with autonomy within clear boundaries. Its activities are often described as:

items: **Evaluate:** assess the organisation, its strategy, portfolio and relationships.
**Direct:** assign responsibility and direct strategy and policy.
**Monitor:** check performance and compliance with policies and direction.

blocks.title: Link to COBIT
blocks.text: The evaluate-direct-monitor pattern is the same as COBIT's EDM domain and ISO/IEC 38500.
The set of interconnected activities an organisation performs to create and deliver valuable products and services; in ITIL (Version 5) described through the Product and Service Lifecycle activities.
A conceptual view of how the organisation works: its structure, capabilities, processes and technology used to achieve its purpose.

The organisation's **purpose** shapes its **operating model**, which is realised through **value chain activities** that draw on **management practices**. Practices provide the capabilities; value chain activities combine them into value streams that respond to demand.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a component of the ITIL Value System?
quiz.explain: Components: guiding principles, governance, value chain, management practices, continual improvement.

quiz.q: Which principle recommends not building everything from scratch?

options: The means by which an organisation is directed and controlled

options: They must be applied in order

quiz.q: Making work visible on shared boards reflects which principle?

chapters.title: Management practices
chapters.summary: What a practice is, the two practice groups, all 34 practices, practice guides and metrics.

blocks.text: A set of organisational resources designed for performing work or accomplishing an objective.

Practices provide the capabilities that value chain activities draw on. A single practice (e.g. incident management) contributes to several lifecycle activities, and each value stream uses several practices.

rows: Adopted from general business management and applied to products and services
Developed in service and product management and IT

blocks.title: Level of detail
blocks.text: Foundation tests the definition of a practice, the two groups, the role of practices in the Value System, and the structure and benefits of practice guides. Purpose-level awareness of individual practices is useful context.

Align practices and services with changing needs through ongoing improvement
Maintain and improve effective, efficient use of information and knowledge
Support good decisions and improvement by reducing uncertainty through data
Ensure changes are implemented smoothly and benefits realised by managing the human side
Ensure the right mix of programmes, projects, products and services to execute strategy within funding
Establish and nurture links with stakeholders at strategic and tactical levels
Formulate goals and adopt courses of action and resources to achieve them
Ensure suppliers and their performance are managed to support seamless delivery
Ensure the right people with the right skills and knowledge are in the right roles
Ensure services deliver agreed levels of availability
Analyse the business, define needs and recommend solutions
Ensure services achieve agreed performance and meet demand cost-effectively
Maximise successful changes by assessing risk, authorising changes and managing the change schedule
Move new or changed components to live or other environments
Minimise the negative impact of incidents by restoring normal service as quickly as possible
Protect information needed to conduct business: confidentiality, integrity, availability
Oversee infrastructure and platforms, including cloud
Plan and manage the full lifecycle of IT assets to maximise value and control costs and risks
Observe services and components, and record and report selected changes of state (events)
Reduce the likelihood and impact of incidents by identifying causes and managing workarounds and known errors
Make new and changed services and features available for use
Provide a single source of consistent information on services and offerings
Ensure accurate, reliable information about the configuration of services and CIs is available when needed
Ensure availability and performance of services are maintained at acceptable levels during a disaster
Design products and services that are fit for purpose, fit for use and deliverable
Capture demand for incident resolution and service requests; the entry point and single point of contact
Support strategies and plans for managing the organisation's finances for services
Set clear business-based targets for service levels and ensure delivery is assessed, monitored and managed against them
Support agreed quality by handling all predefined, user-initiated service requests effectively
Ensure new or changed products and services meet defined requirements
Ensure applications meet stakeholder needs in functionality, reliability, maintainability, compliance and auditability

blocks.title: Grouping changed
blocks.text: In ITIL 4, information security and service financial management were general management practices, and technical management practices were a third group. Version 5 uses two groups. Check the official book if a question hinges on grouping.

**ITIL Practice Guides** give detailed guidance for each practice. They typically cover the purpose, key terms and scope; how the practice contributes to value streams; roles and competencies; information and technology; partners and suppliers; and success factors with key metrics.

items: **Benefits:** consistent language across teams, a ready-made starting point, practical process and role guidance, and a basis for measuring capability.

blocks.text: A measurement or calculation that is monitored or reported for management and improvement.
A necessary precondition for achieving an intended result.

blocks.title: CSF vs metric
blocks.text: For incident management, a CSF could be "incidents are resolved quickly and effectively". Metrics: mean time to restore, % resolved within target, first-contact resolution rate, user satisfaction.

chapters.title: The Continual Improvement Model
chapters.summary: The seven steps and the role of continual improvement in the Value System.

rows: Understand the organisation's vision and objectives; align the initiative
Baseline assessment of the current state
Where do we want to be?
Define measurable target state and outcomes, based on gaps
Execute the plan, iteratively, managing risk and change
Measure results against targets and the vision
How do we keep the momentum going?
Embed changes, recognise success, feed lessons into the next cycle

blocks.title: Link to the principles
blocks.text: Step 2 embodies start where you are. Steps 4-5 embody progress iteratively with feedback. Step 1 and the whole model embody focus on value.

sections.title: Continual improvement in the Value System

blocks.text: Continual improvement is a **component** of the Value System, a **general management practice**, and embedded in every lifecycle activity. Everyone is responsible for it, not just a dedicated team. Improvement initiatives are tracked in a continual improvement register (or similar backlog) and prioritised by value.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: A service desk's first-contact resolution is 48% (where are we now). The target is 65% in 6 months (where do we want to be). The team adds a knowledge base and AI-suggested answers in two-week iterations (take action), measures 61% after 4 months (did we get there), and adds the KB review to routine work (keep momentum).

quiz.q: What is the first step of the Continual Improvement Model?

chapters.title: Value streams
chapters.summary: Core and enabling value streams, complexity thinking, mapping and management.

blocks.text: A series of steps an organisation undertakes to create and deliver products and services to consumers.
A value stream that directly delivers value to external consumers (e.g. onboarding a new customer, restoring a failed service).
A value stream that supports core value streams by providing capabilities or resources internally (e.g. hiring engineers, procuring cloud capacity).
A technique to visualise the flow of work and information through a value stream to identify waste and improvement opportunities.
The ongoing practice of measuring, managing and improving the flow of value through value streams.
Mapping produces the picture; management keeps improving the flow using that picture and live data. Mapping is typically a periodic activity; management is continuous.
Recognising that systems range from clear and complicated (cause and effect can be known) to complex (cause and effect only visible in hindsight), and choosing ways of working to match.

items: **Clear / complicated work** (e.g. provisioning a standard laptop): standardise, document, automate.
**Complex work** (e.g. designing a new digital service, resolving a novel major incident): experiment, use short feedback loops, empower teams, avoid rigid procedures.
Optimising workflows for complexity means not forcing one standard process on every kind of work.

sections.title: Elements of a value stream map

rows: What starts the value stream (e.g. customer request)
Activities performed, with the teams or practices involved
Time actually spent working on a step
Time work sits idle between steps
Total elapsed time from trigger to outcome
Share of work received by a step that doesn't need rework

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: Mapping new employee IT onboarding shows a 12-day lead time with only 5 hours of work; most delay is waiting for manager approvals and hardware. Pre-approved role bundles and stocked devices cut lead time to 2 days.

quiz.q: A value stream that directly delivers value to external consumers is...
Hiring engineers for the delivery teams is an example of a(n)...
quiz.explain: It supports core value streams internally.

quiz.q: Which is the relationship between value stream mapping and management?
options: Mapping visualises the flow; management continually measures and improves it
Management happens once; mapping is continuous

quiz.q: For complex work, which approach fits best?
quiz.explain: Complex work needs probing and feedback.

chapters.title: ITIL and AI
chapters.summary: AI terms, how AI supports the lifecycle and value chain, AI governance and the 6C model.

blocks.text: Technology that enables machines to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as recognising patterns, understanding language, reasoning and making decisions.
How far an organisation has progressed in adopting, integrating and governing AI to create value.
AI that creates new content (text, code, images, audio) based on patterns learned from data.
AI systems that can pursue goals with a degree of autonomy: planning, making decisions and taking actions across tools and systems with limited human intervention.
The frameworks, policies, roles and controls that direct and oversee how AI is developed, used and monitored so that it is responsible, safe, compliant and aligned with objectives.

sections.title: AI across the lifecycle and value chain

rows: Analysing customer feedback and usage data to find opportunities
Generating prototypes, user journeys and test scenarios
Comparing vendor offers and analysing contract risk
Predicting change risk, automating deployment checks
AIOps: anomaly detection, event correlation, predictive capacity
Suggesting known-error workarounds, summarising incidents, root cause hints

blocks.title: Keep humans accountable
blocks.text: AI can automate steps across the lifecycle, but accountability stays with people. Agentic AI in particular needs clear boundaries, approval points and the ability to stop it.
ITIL (Version 5) introduces the **ITIL AI Capability Model** to classify what an AI system does, so that governance and controls fit the capability. The six capabilities:

rows: Generates new content, code or artefacts
Deduplicating the knowledge base, tagging tickets
Explains, summarises and makes information understandable
Summarising a long incident thread for a manager
Analyses, reasons, predicts and supports decisions
Predicting change failure risk, root cause suggestions
Chatbots and virtual agents talking to users
Orchestrates tasks, workflows or other agents
An agent routing tickets and triggering automations

blocks.title: Check the official wording
blocks.text: Third-party descriptions of the 6C capabilities vary. The exam tests understanding (e.g. matching a scenario to a capability), so confirm the official descriptions in the ITIL Foundation (Version 5) book.
A separate **ITIL AI Governance** extension module goes deeper into AI governance, risk profiling of capabilities and controls.

quiz.q: AI that plans and takes actions toward goals with limited human intervention is...
Which is one of the six capabilities in the ITIL AI Capability Model?
quiz.explain: Creation, curation, clarification, cognition, communication, coordination.

quiz.q: A virtual agent chatting with users mainly reflects which capability?
AIOps anomaly detection most supports which lifecycle activity?

chapters.title: ITIL and other frameworks
chapters.summary: How ITIL works with DevOps and PRINCE2.

blocks.text: **DevOps** is a culture and set of practices that bring development and operations together to deliver changes quickly and reliably, using automation, CI/CD, shared ownership and fast feedback.

rows: End-to-end view of value, from discover to support
Shared team ownership ("you build it, you run it")
Practices for incident, problem, change, service level and more

blocks.text: They complement each other: DevOps accelerates build and transition, while ITIL ensures what is deployed is operated, delivered and supported well, and that changes are enabled (not blocked) by risk-based change enablement, e.g. pre-authorised standard changes in the pipeline.

**PRINCE2** is a structured project management method (also owned by PeopleCert). Project management matters in ITIL because many new or significantly changed products and services are delivered through projects, and project management is itself an ITIL practice.

items: PRINCE2 controls the **temporary** effort: business case, stages, roles, tolerances, closure.
ITIL manages the **ongoing** product and service across its lifecycle, before and after the project.
Together: the project delivers the change within time, cost and scope; ITIL ensures the result is transitioned, operated and supported and keeps creating value.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: A PRINCE2 project replaces a bank's contact-centre platform. ITIL practices feed requirements (service level, continuity), accept the release through transition, and own operations after project closure.

quiz.q: How do ITIL and DevOps relate?
options: They are complementary: DevOps accelerates delivery, ITIL covers the full lifecycle and practices

quiz.q: Why is project management important in ITIL?
options: Many new or changed products and services are delivered through projects
quiz.explain: Projects deliver change; ITIL manages the ongoing service.

quiz.q: Which describes PRINCE2's focus?
